title: Monday Starter: Nun leading Caritas Nepal calls for international aid after floods - Global Sisters Report
description: Monday Starter: Nun leading Caritas Nepal calls for international aid after floods  Global Sisters Report
publisher.title: Global Sisters Report
full_article:
With the death toll mounting to more than 1,000 and with more than 4,500 missing, the executive director of Caritas Nepal is warning that the disaster caused by massive flooding in the country on Aug. 26 has not fully played out and will require international support for months to come. "The situation remains extremely alarming, and the number of casualties continues to rise as search and rescue operations are still ongoing," Sr. Cecilia Durga Shrestha, a member of the Sisters of St. Joseph of Cluny and head of Caritas Nepal since 2023, said of Nepal government search, rescue and relief efforts. "Thousands of people have been affected, with many lives lost, people still missing, and significant damage to homes, roads, bridges, livelihoods and other essential infrastructure," Shrestha told GSR, speaking specifically of the flooding that swept through communities in Nuwakot near the Himalayan nation's border with China.

Sr. Cecilia Durga Shrestha, a member of the Sisters of St. Joseph of Cluny, has been serving as executive director of Caritas Nepal since 2023. (Courtesy of Caritas Nepal)

Shrestha said that since the second day of the disaster, Caritas Nepal and its partners have been on the ground accompanying affected communities. "We are providing food and non-food items, essential household utensils, and other emergency supplies," Shrestha said. "We are also supporting people who have lost family members with essential items needed for mourning and funeral rituals, as well as providing medical kits to affected communities in different locations." However, at present, the most urgent needs include temporary shelter, debris clearance, essential household items, temporary learning centers for children, psychosocial counseling, medical assistance and support to restore basic livelihoods and services. Shrestha stressed the need for the international community to continue accompanying affected communities in the coming months. "Financial support would be particularly valuable to enable us to respond to both immediate humanitarian needs and the longer-term recovery and rebuilding of affected families and communities," she said. Nepal has a population of 31 million and is predominantly Hindu, with only about 10,000 Roman Catholics. But Caritas' response, Shrestha said, is to extend a "helping hand to the affected people from the ground," regardless of religious affiliation.

Related: Nepal floods leave 'nothing' behind as Catholic nuns mobilize aid

Loyola University honors the late Sr. Jean Schmidt with campus statue Loyola University Chicago has honored one of its icons, the late Sr. Jean Dolores Schmidt — longtime Loyola Ramblers basketball fan, team chaplain and campus fixture — with a statue on the university's Rogers Park campus. The Aug. 21 unveiling of the cast bronze statue, which depicts Schmidt sitting on a bench and holding a Loyola basketball, fell on what would have been the beloved sister's 107th birthday and a little less than a year since Schmidt's death at age 106 on Oct. 9, 2025. Known to all as Sister Jean, Schmidt received international attention and acclaim during the Loyola Ramblers' appearance during the 2018 NCAA March Madness tournament, the year she served as the team's chaplain at age 98.

Tom Hitcho, Loyola senior associate athletics director and longtime friend of Sr. Jean Schmidt, was the first to sit next to the statue after it was unveiled Aug. 21, 2026, at Loyola University Chicago. (Courtesy of Loyola University Chicago)

But during the statue unveiling ceremony, university officials and members of her congregation, the Sisters of Charity of the Blessed Virgin Mary, praised Schmidt for being more than a dedicated basketball fan. "Sister Jean's ministry of presence was a gift to generations of Ramblers," said Loyola President Mark Reed, who praised Schmidt's compassion, joy and concern and care for students and staff. In her remarks, Sr. LaDonna Manternach, president of the Sisters of Charity of the Blessed Virgin Mary, recalled Schmidt's love of Loyola students. "A good listener, she inspired many to pursue their dreams with purpose. Her deep trust in God guided her life and encouraged others to trust their own journey. "

क्लुनी के सेंट जोसेफ के सिस्टर्स के सदस्य सीनियर सेसिलिया दुर्गा श्रेष्ठ 2023 स कैरिटास नेपाल के कार्यकारी निदेशक के रूप में कार्यरत छैथ।(कैरिटास नेपाल के सौजन्य स)

लोयोला विश्वविद्यालय न॑ कैंपस केरऽ मूर्ति स॑ स्वर्गीय सीनियर जीन श्मिट क॑ सम्मानित करलकै लोयोला यूनिवर्सिटी शिकागो न॑ अपनऽ एगो आइकन, स्वर्गीय सीनियर जीन डोलोरेस श्मिट — लंबा समय स॑ लोयोला रैम्बल्स केरऽ बास्केटबॉल प्रशंसक, टीम केरऽ चपरासी आरू कैंपस फिक्सचर — क॑ विश्वविद्यालय केरऽ रोजर्स पार्क परिसर म॑ एगो मूर्ति के साथ सम्मानित करलकै । 21 अगस्त कए कास्ट कांस्य मूर्ति क अनावरण, जाहि मे श्मिट कए बेंच पर बैसल आ लोयोला बास्केटबॉल पकड़ने देखाउल गेल अछि, जे प्रिय बहिन क 107म जन्मदिन आ 9 अक्टूबर 2025 कए 106 साल क उम्र मे श्मिट क निधन क एक साल स किछु कम समय पर पड़ल 2018 एनसीएए मार्च मैडनेस टूर्नामेंट के दौरान लोयोला रैम्बलर्स केरऽ उपस्थिति के दौरान ध्यान आरू प्रशंसा, जेकरा म॑ हुनी 98 साल के उम्र म॑ टीम केरऽ चपरासी के रूप म॑ काम करलकै ।

लोयोला केरऽ सीनियर एसोसिएट एथलेटिक्स डायरेक्टर आरू सीनियर जीन श्मिट केरऽ लंबा समय स॑ दोस्त टॉम हित्चो न॑ २१ अगस्त २०२६ क॑ लोयोला यूनिवर्सिटी शिकागो म॑ एकरऽ अनावरण के बाद सबसें पहलऽ मूर्ति के बगल म॑ बैठलऽ छेलै । (लोयोला विश्वविद्यालय शिकागो के सौजन्य)

लेकिन मूर्ति के अनावरण समारोह के दौरान विश्वविद्यालय के अधिकारी आरू हुनकऽ मंडली के सदस्य, सिस्टर्स ऑफ चैरिटी ऑफ द ब्लेसड वर्जिन मैरी न॑ श्मिट के प्रशंसा करलकै कि हुनी एगो समर्पित बास्केटबॉल प्रशंसक स॑ भी अधिक छै । लोयोला केरऽ अध्यक्ष मार्क रीड न॑ कहलकै कि सिस्टर जीन केरऽ उपस्थिति मंत्रालय रैम्बलर केरऽ पीढ़ी लेली एगो उपहार छेलै, जेकरा न॑ श्मिट केरऽ करुणा, खुशी आरू चिंता आरू छात्र आरू कर्मचारी केरऽ देखभाल के प्रशंसा करलकै । अपनऽ टिप्पणी म॑ सिस्टर्स ऑफ चैरिटी ऑफ द ब्लेसड वर्जिन मैरी केरऽ अध्यक्ष सीनियर लाडोना मंटरनच न॑ श्मिट केरऽ लोयोला केरऽ छात्रऽ के प्रति प्रेम के याद करलकै । "एकटा नीक श्रोता, ओ बहुतो केँ अपन सपना केँ उद्देश्य सँ पूरा करबाक लेल प्रेरित केलनि। भगवान पर हुनकर गहींर भरोसा हुनकर जीवन केँ मार्गदर्शन केलक आ दोसरो केँ अपन यात्रा पर भरोसा करबाक लेल प्रोत्साहित केलक।"

title: Nepal floods: Death toll climbs to 1,355 as rescue efforts continue; nearly 5,000 still missing - The Hindu
description: Nepal floods: Death toll climbs to 1,355 as rescue efforts continue; nearly 5,000 still missing  The Hindu
publisher.title: The Hindu
full_article:
The death toll from the devastating flash floods in Nepal surged to 1,355 on Monday (September 7, 2026) as more bodies were recovered from the affected areas, authorities said.

Rescue teams continued to search for 4,996 people, including at least 589 foreign nationals, who remain missing, while 13,396 people have been rescued so far, the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) said.

Nepal flash floods: Death toll rises to 1,344

According to NDRRMA, 363 bodies have been recovered from Chitwan district, 221 from Nawalparasi West, 222 from Nawalparasi East and 197 from Nuwakot.

Similarly, 169 bodies were recovered from Rasuwa, 75 from Gorkha, 70 from Dhading and 38 from Tanahu, it said.

The joint command of security forces is actively conducting search and rescue operations.

Major rescue operations are underway at hydropower projects in flood-affected districts, where hundreds of men are believed to be trapped in tunnels. Teams of experts from India and China are assisting their Nepali counterparts in these operations.

The flash floods, triggered by an ice-rock avalanche near the Nepal-Tibet border on August 26, devastated towns and villages in northern and central Nepal.

Nepal flash floods 2026 Nepal observes national mourning on 13th day of flash flood tragedy

The Bhotekoshi River, which flows south from the Himalayan border region, carried the floodwaters downstream, sweeping away homes, vehicles, roads and bridges and damaging hydropower projects.

The disaster also killed at least 21 people on the Chinese side, while more than 500 people remain missing in Tibet, according to Chinese media reports.

title: Nepal mourns flood victims as hopes persist for workers trapped in tunnels - TRT World
description: Nepal mourns flood victims as hopes persist for workers trapped in tunnels  TRT World
publisher.title: TRT World
full_article:
Nepal held a national day of mourning on Monday for victims of devastating glacial floods, as families of missing hydropower workers feared trapped in tunnels prayed rescuers might yet find them alive.

The August 26 glacial and mountain collapse on the China-Nepal border killed at least 1,398 people, with more than 5,500 missing, including around 800 foreigners.

Flags flew at half-mast, with candlelight vigils planned later in the day, following traditional Hindu mourning rituals on the 13th day after death.

Hundreds of hydropower workers are among the missing, but the rescue of three of them from deep inside tunnels, two Nepalis on Friday and a Chinese man on Saturday, have buoyed hopes that more could still be alive.

Nepal Army spokesman Raja Ram Basnet told AFP on Monday that rescue efforts were continuing "with the same tempo we had on day one".

"Our focus is on search and rescue at three levels, on ground, by air, and in the tunnels," he said.

"We are making sure that no one is still stranded."

Entire communities have been swept away, roads destroyed, and homes demolished.

'Hope'

But families of some of the missing workers who gathered in the capital Kathmandu said the government must move faster.

"We have a lot of hope," said Reena Amatya Shrestha, whose brother is among the missing.

"They say they are doing rescue. If the rescue is there, where's the result? We need the result."

Related TRT World - Rescuers pull Chinese national alive from Nepal tunnel after 10 days

Australian tunnel rescue expert Arnold Dix, who is advising Nepali teams, said the operation presented an unprecedented challenge.

"We are facing something I have never faced before," said Dix, president of the International Tunnelling and Underground Space Association, in a post on social media.

"Not one rescue, but multiple potential rescues, unfolding at the same time, in different places, each with its own dangers, uncertainties, and lives that may still be saved."

नेपाल सेना के प्रवक्ता राजा राम बस्नेट सोमदिन एएफपी के कहलनि जे, बचाव के प्रयास जारी अछि, जेना पहिल दिन छल।

ओ कहला जे हमर ध्यान तीन स्तर पर, जमीन पर, हवाई मार्ग स आ सुरंग मे खोज आ बचाव पर अछि।

title: Some Nepal villages so devastated, you’d think they never existed, says Malaysian relief volunteer - Yahoo
description: Some Nepal villages so devastated, you’d think they never existed, says Malaysian relief volunteer  Yahoo
publisher.title: Yahoo
full_article:
KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 7 — Some villages in Nepal have been so completely devastated by the floods that there is no sign they ever existed, according to Malaysian relief volunteers who have seen the destruction first-hand.

Mercy Malaysia Rapid Assessment Team leader Vivegananthan Rajangam said some settlements along the rivers were left without a single house after the floods tore through Benighat, Nuwakot and Bidur.

"The damage is very severe. In some villages, there isn't even one house left. If someone went there for the first time, they would think there was no village there," he told Harian Metro today.

"In many places hit by the floods along the river, nobody lives there anymore. In some places, there is no trace of any houses at all."

Even concrete buildings were not spared, with only about 20 per cent of such structures still standing in some settlements, he said.

"Most of these concrete buildings were also swept away," Vivegananthan recounted.

Survivors have since been moved away from the worst-hit areas, with many evacuated to Kathmandu and Nuwakot and housed in schools and halls on higher ground.

Vivegananthan said the Nepali authorities had also set up temporary shelters for those who survived the floods.

In Nuwakot alone, 19 such shelters have been established, he said.

Based on discussions with local authorities and assessments on the ground, food supplies at the shelters were adequate, but survivors needed other forms of assistance.

Mercy Malaysia's three-member team will remain in Nepal for about 10 days to assess how best to support those who survived the disaster.

Vivegananthan stressed that the team was not involved in search and rescue operations but was focused on helping survivors rebuild their lives.

"We are not involved in search and rescue. We are here to help those who survived," he said.

Among the assistance provided are medicines, cooking equipment and toys for children, which are being channelled through Nepali authorities, including the country's Health Ministry.

"The assistance we provide is aimed at helping them continue their lives as best as possible so they can return to normal," Vivegananthan said.

full_article:
Eleven days after catastrophic flooding along the Nepal-China border killed more than 1,300 people and left thousands missing, hundreds of workers are still believed to be trapped in tunnels at hydropower sites buried by mudslides.

Former Haymarket Town Council member Madhu Panthi and the Manassas-based America Nepal Helping Society are asking for support.

“In the world, I’d like to humbly request if there is any equipment that can dig and to open the tunnel … you know more than 5,000 people are missing. And what is the best mechanism to save their life? That’s what we are looking for,” Panthi said.

Panthi moved to Northern Virginia from Nepal in 2001 and helped coordinate donations and disaster response efforts after a 7.8 magnitude earthquake killed thousands and damaged more than 1 million homes and buildings in Nepal in 2015.

“That earthquake also did lots of damage. But earthquake, you can remove the debris and you can find the people in there. But this one is, you know, wiping out everything, and now the roads are not there. The bridges are not there. House, school and everything, everything is destroyed and wiped away,” Panthi said

The nonprofit has set an initial goal of raising $100,000 to support emergency shelter, food, water, health services and other relief efforts. As of Sunday, it had raised more than $52,000.

Panthi said the group is working with the Embassy of Nepal in D.C. and the Nepalese government, to help determine where the money is needed most.

According to the organization’s website, all donations are “subject to due diligence and final approval” and that the money “may support Government of Nepal disaster-relief funds identified in the Government’s 26 August appeal and/or other qualified humanitarian recipients.”

“They can donate by credit card. They can send by check. And all money goes 100% to the victims of Nepal: their food, their shelter, their medical, you know, their clothes, their livelihood,” Panthi said.

Panthi, who said one of his closest friends remains among the missing, told WTOP that ANHS is not sending rescue teams to the disaster area, unlike after Nepal’s 2015 earthquake when some of the group’s members went to distribute aid alongside Fairfax County Fire and Rescue personnel deployed with USAID’s Disaster Assistance Response Team.

Instead, the group is focused on raising money and working within Nepal’s “one door policy,” which is intended to streamline relief distribution and prevent aid from being unevenly distributed. “We don’t want to, you know, send somebody and then some area-people are not getting [help], and some area-people have too much,” Panthi said.

Panthi said that’s another reason ANHS is so focused on its financial goal to help Nepal: “Our heart, our brain, our everything is there. Our family are there. What can we do?”

Last week, PKP Tender Hearts Foundation, an area group dedicated to preserving Nepalese culture and serving communities in Nepal, held a candlelight vigil in Fairfax County with the George Mason University’s Nepalese Student Association to raise money and awareness for the flood victims.

People interested in donating to the America Nepal Helping Society’s disaster relief fund can do so through the organization’s website.

title: China Falls Victim To Own Secrecy After Nepal’s Deadly Floods - Newsweek
description: China Falls Victim To Own Secrecy After Nepal’s Deadly Floods  Newsweek
publisher.title: Newsweek
full_article:
China finds itself fighting an information war over its strategic interests in the Himalayas after last month’s devastating flash floods on the Nepal-Tibet border put a spotlight on a major hydropower megaproject near India—over 600 miles away and still shrouded in secrecy.

Flooding triggered by a glacial collapse on August 26 claimed over 1,300 lives and up to four times that are still missing, including dozens of Americans. The U.S. Geological Survey said the Lhenda and Trishuli rivers carried glacial debris—ice, water, boulders and later rubble—approximately 62 miles downslope into central Nepal.

China has no hydropower stations upstream, and its infrastructure projects could have played no part in the ice avalanche, the latest assessments suggest. But China is the main contributor of civil engineering works along the riverbanks, so experts speculate that its bridges, highways and buildings in the valley may have altered the speed and composition of the debris flow.

Read More on World

While China and its neighbor India vie for influence over Nepal, Beijing’s skeptics in New Delhi say the worst disaster of its kind in the Himalayas should serve as a warning about Chinese hydropower plans elsewhere in Tibet and their effects downstream. China is fighting back.

When Disaster Strikes

Preliminary reports aided by satellite imagery said the landslide likely began at an elevation of over 17,000 feet, on the northern slope of the Langtang Lirung mountain in Nepal. The collapsing glacier crashed into the valley floor at such a force that it registered as a magnitude 5.2 earthquake, according to the U.S. Geological Survey.

The first images of the torrent of mud and floodwater came from surveillance cameras at China’s Gyirong port, which was washed away in a matter of seconds. The border crossing was the main land route for China’s trade with Nepal.

For those living and working in the path of the floods, what little forewarning there was had come too late. Satellite imagery provided by Planet showed the destruction left behind by the fast-moving floodwater, like a giant scar in the earth.

...

When disaster strikes, Beijing’s first reaction is containment, of the damage but also of information.

Within hours of the flooding, videos filmed by witnesses were censored on Chinese social media apps almost as quickly as they were being uploaded. Only approved state media footage remained, as well as any videos that made it out of China’s Great Firewall.

It took the Chinese government 11 days to permit foreign media to report from the Gyirong border area. Beijing’s intense need for control created an informative vacuum in which unfavorable narratives bloomed.

One widely quoted statement came from Madhav Prasad Chaulagain, the former Nepalese environment minister, who said China had failed to warn Nepal about the floods. The comments made to an Indian broadcaster fed critics for days over Beijing’s alleged reluctance to share hydrological data.

Nepalese officials sought environmental monitoring data from Chinese counterparts—including on glacier-related hazards—three months before the disaster but never received it, Reuters reported.

"The broader lesson for the rest of the world is that China’s censorship and cover-ups should not be dismissed as problems affecting only the Chinese people. Opacity does not stay within national borders. Sooner or later, people elsewhere may also bear the costs," Henry Gao, a professor of law at Singapore Management University, said on X.

"The international community should press China to become more transparent and accountable. But meaningful accountability will remain elusive unless China undertakes fundamental political reform and becomes a democracy," Gao said.

China controls the rivers upstream, and water level information can be considered strategically sensitive. Nepal says it will rebuild an early warning system on its border with China utilizing sensors and cameras, but there’s every chance its neighbor will push back.

After Indian and Nepalese social media users on X said China’s lack of transparency was to blame for the deadly floods, the Chinese embassy in Kathmandu fired back, saying the allegations were designed to disrupt China’s cooperation with Nepal.

Chinese authorities, responding to concerns about an information blackout that could cost lives, said they were already sharing whatever data they had. China’s state broadcaster CCTV said glaciers often move and were difficult to predict before collapse.

...

The Himalayas are warming at twice the global average, experts say, making it vulnerable to environmental catastrophes including landslides and floods.

Last week, the Chinese ambassador to Nepal, Zhang Maoming, shared an op-ed written by a Chinese professor in the government-owned newspaper Rising Nepal Daily , which shifted blame for the disaster onto the West.

"The warming in Nepal and the Tibetan Plateau isn't the result of local emissions—it's the accumulated, centuries-old carbon emissions of the industrialized Global North that are bearing down on a cryosphere both countries depend on for their water security," it said.

The Damage Is Done

China’s leaders know the dangers of a runaway narrative, about a palace coup or the instability of the Communist Party’s rule. Its censorship was only partly to do with not wanting to look bad.

Externally, Beijing would’ve been aware of what the disaster meant for its role as a reliable economic partner to Nepal and other developing countries. Internally, its response would speak to its ability to safely manage the region of Tibet, a source of tension with New Delhi, which has hosted the 14th Dalai Lama in exile in northern India for nearly seven decades.

China’s preference for secrecy, however, could cause the greatest damage to its interests in eastern Tibet, where it’s building the world’s largest dam on a river that sustains tens of millions of lives downstream.

The Medog hydropower project, which began last year and will run into the 2030s, will solidify Chinese control of the Yarlung Tsangpo, the critical freshwater source of the Brahmaputra in India and later the Jamuna in Bangladesh.

Nearly a dozen dams of varying sizes have already been built in the eastern parts of politically sensitive Tibet, a geologically fragile region known for devastating earthquakes in the past.

"The geological danger is only part of the story. China is increasingly transforming its control of the Tibetan Plateau—the source of most of Asia’s major rivers—into strategic leverage," Brahma Chellaney, a professor of strategic studies at the Center for Policy Research, a New Delhi think tank, said in an analysis written before the glacial collapse in Nepal.

"It has built cascades of dams on transboundary rivers, withheld hydrological data during periods of tension, and resisted entering any water-sharing treaty with downstream states. Water has become another instrument of coercive statecraft," Chellaney said.

The Chinese government has invited additional scrutiny of its "project of the century" because it won’t disclose further details about the scale of the super dam.

"A secretive Chinese project in my eyes means it’s hard for anyone to find credible information about it, even in Chinese. That is the case for the now under-construction hydropower mega-project on the Yarlung Tsangpo River in eastern Tibet," Shanghai-based energy analyst David Fishman said in a recent Substack newsletter.

China says the $170 billion dam will generate 60 gigawatts of electricity, three times that of the Three Gorges Dam in central China—the largest hydropower facility in the world.

"Yet for all the fanfare about the project’s ambitious scale, the public knows very little about what kind of facility it even is, never mind details like the construction milestones, power export destinations, effects on the surrounding environment, or expected impact on human populations," Fishman said.

Since the disaster in Nepal, Indian social media users on X and other commentators have described China’s mega dam as a "time bomb" that could threaten India.

China may disagree but its reluctance to share information means it’s letting others control the narrative.

चीन के कहना छै कि 170 अरब डॉलर के ई बांध स॑ 60 गीगावाट बिजली पैदा होतै, जे मध्य चीन केरऽ थ्री गॉर्ज डैम स॑ तीन गुना अधिक छै – जे दुनिया केरऽ सबस॑ बड़ऽ जलविद्युत सुविधा छै ।

फिशमैन न॑ कहलकै कि तभियो ई परियोजना केरऽ महत्वाकांक्षी पैमाना के बारे म॑ जेतना धूमधाम छै, ओकरा लेली जनता क॑ ई बात के बारे म॑ बहुत कम जानकारी छै कि ई केना सुविधा भी छै, निर्माण केरऽ मील के पत्थर, बिजली निर्यात गंतव्य, आसपास के पर्यावरण प॑ पड़ै वाला प्रभाव, या मानव आबादी प॑ अपेक्षित प्रभाव जैसनऽ विवरण के बात क॑ कभियो नै ।

नेपाल केरऽ आपदा के बाद स॑ एक्स प॑ भारतीय सोशल मीडिया यूजर आरू अन्य कमेंटेटर न॑ चीन केरऽ मेगा डैम क॑ एगो “टाइम बम” बतैलकै जेकरा स॑ भारत प॑ खतरा पैदा होय सकै छै ।

चीन एहि बात सं असहमत भ’ सकैत अछि मुदा जानकारी साझा करबा मे ओकर अनिच्छा के मतलब अछि जे ओ दोसर के कथ्य पर नियंत्रण राखय दैत अछि.

प्रतिस्पर्धी हिमालय पर आपसी विश्वास कम अछि, आ ई कम होमय बला अछि.
